title: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
summary: Measure what each stage of a retrieve-then-rerank pipeline contributes: add-one-in vs leave-one-out, a fixed harness, per-query paired tests, interaction effects, Shapley attribution and honest reporting.
outcomes: Explain why add-one-in and leave-one-out ablations can rank the same stages differently
List what must stay fixed in an ablation (queries, qrels, candidate depth, seeds, tuning budget)
Compute per-query deltas, an exact paired randomization p-value, a confidence interval and an effect size
Detect interaction effects between stages and compute Shapley values that split a total gain
Write an ablation table with deltas, intervals, tests, cost and the settings that were held fixed

lessons.title: One final score hides where the gain came from

blocks.md:
You built a multi-stage pipeline: a cheap first stage retrieves candidates, then one or more rerankers reorder them. The final nDCG@10 went up. Which stage earned it? A single end-to-end number cannot say. Some stages may carry the whole gain, some may add nothing but latency, and some may only help when another stage is present.

An **ablation study** answers that question by running the same evaluation on variants of the system with components removed (ablated) or added one at a time, and comparing the scores on the same queries.

Lipton and Steinhardt list **failure to identify the sources of empirical gains** as one of four troubling trends in ML papers. In their words, too frequently authors propose many tweaks absent proper ablation studies, and sometimes just one of the changes is actually responsible for the improved results. They cite Melis et al., who found that gains attributed to newer, more complex network architectures were actually due to better hyperparameter tuning: on equal footing, vanilla LSTMs topped the leaderboard.

They also note that ablation is neither necessary nor sufficient for understanding a method, so treat it as one tool next to error analysis and robustness checks.

blocks.title: monoBERT and duoBERT stage by stage (MS MARCO dev, MRR@10)

scenes.caption: Nogueira et al. (2019) report each stage of their pipeline as its own row. The first stage alone, Anserini BM25, scores 18.7 MRR@10 on the MS MARCO dev set.
Adding monoBERT, a pointwise BERT reranker over the top 1000 BM25 candidates, roughly doubles the score to 37.2. This one stage carries most of the gain.
Adding duoBERT, a pairwise reranker over monoBERT's top 50 with SUM aggregation, adds 1.0 more (38.2). Target corpus pretraining (TCP) adds another 0.8 (39.0).
The same duoBERT stage with MAX aggregation scores 32.6, below monoBERT alone. A stage is not good or bad by itself: its configuration decides whether it helps or hurts.

blocks.md:
Two more published examples show the pattern. The SPLADE v2 paper reports MRR@10 on MS MARCO dev for SPLADE (0.322), then with max pooling (SPLADE-max, 0.340), then with distillation added (DistilSPLADE-max, 0.368), so a reader can see each change's share. ColBERTv2 tests its residual compression separately on a vanilla ColBERT model: 36.2 MRR@10 uncompressed, 36.2 with 2-bit compression and 35.5 with 1-bit, which isolates compression from the paper's other change, denoised supervision.

Note what these tables show and what they do not: mean deltas on one query set, without per-query detail or intervals. The rest of this course adds those.

blocks.title: The toy pipeline used in this course

scenes.caption: Baseline: BM25 alone returns the top 100 candidates. Every other stage is optional, so there are 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16 possible configurations.
Q rewrites the query before retrieval. H adds a dense retriever whose results are fused with BM25, at the same candidate depth of 100.
R rescores all 100 candidates with a cross-encoder. P reorders R's top 10 with a pairwise model, like duoBERT on top of monoBERT.
All four stages on: mean nDCG@10 is 0.701 over 20 queries, up 0.251 from BM25. The rest of the course asks how to split that 0.251 among Q, H, R and P.

blocks.md: The toy's per-query nDCG@10 values are simulated from a stated model with a fixed seed (stage effects that vary by query, plus small noise), so every number is reproducible. Real pipelines have the same structure but messier effects.

An ablation turns one end-to-end number into a per-component account: what each stage adds, on the same queries and labels, under the same settings. Without it, you cannot tell which stage earns its latency.

blocks.question: A paper adds a new reranker, a new loss and a larger hyperparameter search at once, and reports one final score that beats the baseline. What is the main problem Lipton and Steinhardt would point to?
options: The score should have been reported as MRR instead of nDCG
Rerankers cannot be compared with first-stage retrievers
Readers cannot tell which change caused the gain; it may come entirely from the tuning
The baseline must always be the strongest published system
blocks.explain: Bundling changes hides the source of the gain. Melis et al. found exactly this for LSTM language models: gains credited to architectures came from tuning. Separate rows for each change (or at least for the tuning alone) would show it.

lessons.title: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness

blocks.md:
There are two basic single-component designs:

- **Add-one-in**: start from the baseline (here BM25) and add one stage at a time. The delta answers: what does this stage do on its own?
- **Leave-one-out**: start from the full system and remove one stage at a time. The delta answers: what would we lose by dropping this stage now?

The published tables in lesson 1 are a third design, **cumulative**: add stages in one fixed order and report each step. That is cheap, but each delta depends on what was already added.

Removing a stage is not always a clean subtraction. You must decide what replaces it: no rewrite at all, or a trivial rewrite; BM25 alone, or BM25 with more candidates to keep the reranker's input size equal. State the replacement, because different choices give different deltas.

blocks.title: Leave-one-out: dim one stage, rerun the same 20 queries

scenes.caption: Full system: mean nDCG@10 0.701. This is the reference point for leave-one-out.
Drop Q (the raw query goes to both retrievers): 0.696. Losing the rewrite costs only 0.005 once H is present.
Drop H (BM25 alone fills the same 100 slots): 0.613, a loss of 0.088.
Drop R (P reorders the first-stage top 10 directly): 0.514, a loss of 0.187, the largest single removal.
Drop P (R's order is final): 0.669, a loss of 0.032.

blocks.prompt: Added alone to BM25, Q raises mean nDCG@10 from 0.450 to 0.496. Removed from the full system, it costs only 0.005. P alone changes BM25 from 0.450 to 0.442. Before revealing: what will the two designs say about P, and why do they disagree about Q?
blocks.reveal:
P **hurts** when added alone (-0.009; deltas here use unrounded means, so they can differ by 0.001 from the rounded scores) but **helps** when removed from the full system (-0.032 without it, so it adds +0.032). A pairwise reranker built to polish a cross-encoder's top 10 does not help on a raw BM25 order.

Q helps alone (+0.045) but adds almost nothing on top of H (+0.005). Both Q and H fix the same failure, vocabulary mismatch between query and documents, so once H is there Q is largely redundant. Neither design is wrong; they answer different questions.

blocks.title: Same stages, two designs (mean nDCG@10 delta, 20 queries)

scenes.caption: Add-one-in from BM25: R +0.093, H +0.069, Q +0.045, and P -0.009. On this view P looks harmful and Q looks useful.
Leave-one-out from the full system: R +0.187, H +0.088, P +0.032, and Q only +0.005. R and H count for more here because each helps the other (lesson 4). Deltas come from unrounded means.

blocks.md: Add-one-in measures a stage in isolation; leave-one-out measures its marginal value in the system you will ship. When the two disagree, the stages interact, and that disagreement is itself a finding worth reporting.

blocks.question: You ablate the dense retriever H. To keep latency equal, the no-H variant sends the top 50 BM25 candidates to the reranker instead of the top 100. nDCG drops by 0.09. What can you conclude?
options: H is worth 0.09 nDCG, since latency was held constant
The 0.09 mixes two changes, losing H and halving the candidate depth, so H's own contribution is unknown
H is worth more than 0.09, because more candidates always hurt rerankers
Nothing, because leave-one-out is invalid for first-stage retrievers
blocks.explain: Candidate depth changes recall, which bounds what the reranker can do. Run no-H at depth 100 to isolate H, and report latency separately; a depth-for-latency tradeoff is a second experiment.

blocks.question: Your full pipeline's reranker was tuned for two weeks; the no-reranker variant's BM25 parameters were never tuned. Which harness rule does this violate?
options: Same qrels
Same metric cutoff
Same candidate depth
Same tuning budget for each variant
blocks.explain: Unequal tuning credits effort, not design, to the tuned stage. This is the Melis et al. finding from lesson 1: on equal tuning footing, the simpler model won.

lessons.title: Per-query deltas, paired tests and confidence intervals

blocks.md:
Is the +0.005 from Q real or noise? The ranking-metrics course introduced paired tests over queries; here we apply them to ablations. The key move is to keep the **per-query** scores of both variants and look at the 20 differences $d_i = \text{full}_i - \text{ablated}_i$, rather than at two means.

Pairing removes query difficulty from the comparison. In the toy, BM25 scores range from 0.246 to 0.606 across queries; that spread is much larger than most stage effects, and it cancels out when each query is compared with itself.

blocks.title: Leave-one-out of Q, query by query (nDCG@10)

scenes.caption: Each column is one query run through both variants on the same harness. The mean delta is +0.005.
Coloring by sign: Q wins on 13 queries and loses on 7. Some losses are large (query 6: -0.065), so the small mean hides real movement.
Grouping by query type: on the 11 vocabulary-mismatch queries (tone a) Q adds +0.028 on average; on the other 9 it costs -0.022. The mean averages two opposite effects.

blocks.md:
The **paired randomization test** asks: if Q made no difference, the labels full and without-Q would be interchangeable within each query, so each $d_i$ could equally have been $-d_i$. Flip the signs of the deltas in every possible way, recompute the mean each time, and count how often its absolute value is at least the observed one.

Smucker, Allan and Carterette describe this test for IR and estimated it with 100,000 random permutations for 50 topics. With 20 queries there are only $2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$ sign patterns, so we can enumerate all of them and get the exact p-value.

blocks.code:
import itertools
import numpy as np

def paired_randomization(full, ablated):
    # deltas in thousandths so the comparison is exact
    d = np.rint((np.array(full) - np.array(ablated)) * 1000).astype(np.int64)
    signs = np.array(list(itertools.product([1, -1], repeat=len(d))))
    null = signs @ d                 # sum of deltas under every relabeling
    return (np.abs(null) >= abs(d.sum())).mean()

# Q leave-one-out: 475,996 of 1,048,576 patterns, p = 0.454
# P leave-one-out: 2 of 1,048,576 patterns, p = 1.9e-06
blocks.caption: Exact two-sided paired randomization test by full enumeration. Comparing sums is equivalent to comparing means because n is fixed.

blocks.title: Null distribution of the mean delta for Q (all 2^20 sign flips)

scenes.caption: Share of the 1,048,576 sign patterns whose mean delta falls in each 0.005-wide bin. Under the null, means near zero are most common.
The observed mean, +0.0053, sits in the +0.005 bin. Patterns at least that far from zero in either direction make up 45.4% (exact count, not read from the bins): p = 0.454. No evidence that Q helps.

blocks.md:
Contrast with P. Its leave-one-out deltas are positive on all 20 queries, so only two sign patterns (the observed one and its mirror) are as extreme: $p = 2/2^{20} \approx 1.9 \times 10^{-6}$. The paired t-test agrees closely with the randomization test on both: p = 0.453 for Q, and below 0.0001 for P.

Now ignore the pairing and compare the two lists of 20 scores with an unpaired (Welch) t-test: for P the p-value becomes 0.48. The same data looks like noise, because the spread between queries (standard deviations of 0.137 and 0.147) swamps a consistent +0.032.

blocks.caption: Left: 95% confidence interval for the mean delta ($s_d$ is the standard deviation of the deltas). Right: the standardized effect size Sakai computes for a paired t-test.

blocks.md:
For the toy, with $n = 20$ and $t_{0.975,19} \approx 2.093$:

- **Q** (leave-one-out): $\bar d = 0.005$, $s_d = 0.031$, 95% CI from -0.009 to +0.020, effect size 0.17. The interval includes zero and also includes gains four times the estimate: the experiment cannot tell.
- **P** (leave-one-out): $\bar d = 0.032$, $s_d = 0.024$, 95% CI from +0.021 to +0.043, effect size 1.36.

Report the interval, not just the p-value: it says how big the effect could plausibly be.

Queries are not the only noise source. If a stage is trained, its score also varies with the random seed. Use the same seeds and checkpoints for every stage you are not ablating, and when the ablated stage itself is retrained, run several seeds and report the spread, or a seed-to-seed swing can masquerade as a component effect.

blocks.question: A colleague's ablation script sorts each run's per-query scores from best to worst before running a paired t-test. The test reports p < 0.001 for a stage. What went wrong?
options: Sorting broke the pairing: deltas now compare different queries, so the p-value is meaningless
Nothing; a paired t-test is invariant to the order of the queries
The t-test should have been replaced by the Wilcoxon signed-rank test
The p-value is fine but should be divided by the number of queries
blocks.explain: Pairing works only if position i holds the same query in both runs. Sorting each run separately pairs the best query of one run with the best of the other, removing query-level noise artificially. Align runs by query id before differencing.

blocks.question: Stage X has leave-one-out mean delta +0.004 on 20 queries, 95% CI from -0.011 to +0.019, p = 0.55. What is the best conclusion?
options: X has no effect and can be removed
X helps, since the mean delta is positive
The data are consistent with X hurting slightly or helping moderately; more queries are needed to decide
The test failed because 20 queries is below the minimum for a randomization test
blocks.explain: A non-significant result is not proof of zero effect. The interval spans small losses and gains several times the estimate. Whether to drop X then depends on its cost, which lesson 5 adds to the table.

blocks.md:
Two stages **interact** when the effect of one depends on whether the other is present. In a cascade this is common: a reranker can only promote relevant documents that the first stage put in its candidate list, so a first stage with better recall gives the reranker more to work with.

With four on/off stages there are 16 configurations. Evaluating all of them (a full factorial grid) shows every interaction directly.

scenes.caption: Rows set the front of the pipeline (Q, H), columns the rerankers (R, P). The corners are BM25 (0.450) and the full system (0.701).
R without H: 0.450 to 0.543, +0.093. R with H: 0.519 to 0.668, +0.149. The reranker gains 0.056 more on top of the better first stage: a positive interaction.
P only helps after R: P alone moves BM25 from 0.450 to 0.442, while P after R moves 0.543 to 0.569. Ablating P without R would wrongly call it harmful.
Q and H overlap: Q adds +0.045 without H (0.450 to 0.496) but about +0.002 with H (0.519 to 0.521). A negative interaction: both fix vocabulary mismatch.

blocks.caption: v(S) is mean nDCG@10 with the stages in S on and the others off. A difference of differences: zero means the effects simply add. Computed from unrounded means.

blocks.title: Cumulative tables depend on the order you add stages

scenes.caption: Order Q, H, R, P: Q +0.045, H +0.025, R +0.148, P +0.032. Q looks substantial and H modest.
Order R, P, H, Q on the same 16 runs: R +0.093, P +0.026, H +0.127, Q +0.005. H now looks five times larger and Q nearly useless. Both tables sum to 0.251.

blocks.md: Every order is a valid accounting of the same total, which is why one cumulative table can mislead. The **Shapley value** from cooperative game theory removes the dependence on order: it averages each stage's marginal contribution over all $n!$ orders in which the stages could be added. Treat the stages as players and $v(S)$ as the payoff of coalition $S$. This is the classic formula that Lundberg and Lee restate in the SHAP paper (there, the players are input features).

blocks.caption: For n = 4 stages the weights are 1/4 for S empty, 1/12 for each of the three S of size 1 and of size 2, and 1/4 for S = all other three stages.

blocks.title: Three attributions of the same 0.251 gain

scenes.caption: Add-one-in deltas: they sum to 0.199, not 0.251, because the positive interactions (H with R, R with P) are counted for no one.
Leave-one-out deltas: they sum to 0.312, more than the total, because each interaction is credited to both partners.
Shapley values: Q +0.025, H +0.077, R +0.139, P +0.011. They sum to the total gain (0.252 here after rounding each value; 0.251 exactly), so each stage gets a share: R 55%, H 31%, Q 10%, P 4%.

blocks.md: Shapley values are a summary, not a full account. They need $v$ for all $2^n$ configurations (16 here; for many components, sampled orders are the usual approximation). They hide that P is harmful without R, and they average over queries. Report the interaction cells and per-query spread too.

If two stages interact, no single number per stage tells the whole story. Test the key combinations (a 2 x 2 grid for a suspected pair), and when you need a per-stage split of the total, use Shapley values, which sum exactly to the full-minus-baseline gain.

blocks.question: A team ablates its pairwise reranker by adding it directly to BM25 and finds it lowers nDCG. In production it always runs after a cross-encoder. What should they do?
options: Remove the pairwise reranker, since it hurts
Ablate it in the context where it runs: compare cross-encoder alone vs cross-encoder plus pairwise, with the same candidate depths
Report the add-one-in result as its Shapley value
Move the pairwise reranker before the cross-encoder
blocks.explain: P depends on R (an interaction). In the toy, P is -0.009 on BM25 but +0.026 after R and +0.032 in the full system. The decision-relevant ablation is the one in the shipped context.

blocks.question: Stages A and B both fix the same failure, so they are almost fully redundant. Each adds +0.04 alone, and together they add +0.045. What do leave-one-out deltas show?
options: Both look nearly useless (about +0.005 each), even though removing both costs 0.045
Both look worth +0.04 each
A looks worth +0.045 and B worth 0
Leave-one-out cannot be computed for redundant stages
blocks.explain: Removing either one leaves the other to cover the failure, so each loses only 0.045 - 0.04 = 0.005. Leave-one-out undercounts redundant stages; Shapley gives each +0.0225 here. This is Q and H in the toy.

lessons.title: Reporting an ablation people can trust

blocks.md: Sakai's review of 840 SIGIR and 215 TOIS papers (2006 to 2015) found that over half of the papers with significance tests reported neither p-values nor test statistics, and that the situation was not improving. Sakai argues for reporting p-values and effect sizes, because saying "significant at 0.05" leads to dichotomous thinking. The paper also notes that with enough topics any tiny difference becomes significant, and that too few topics miss real differences: Sakai's topic set size design suggests about 300 topics for a paired t-test to reliably detect a 0.05 difference in MAP with 80% power.

blocks.title: How many queries to pin down a small delta?

scenes.caption: With Q's spread of deltas (s = 0.031), the interval half-width falls as 1/sqrt(n). Simplified: normal approximation, assuming the spread stays the same as queries are added.
To resolve an effect as small as 0.005 (half-width below 0.005), you need about (1.96 x 0.031 / 0.005)^2, roughly 148 queries. The toy's 20 queries give about 0.014.
Less noisy deltas need fewer queries: with s = 0.0235 (P's spread) even 20 queries pin the delta to about plus or minus 0.01. Pairing helps by shrinking s.

blocks.md: **Many variants means many tests.** The 16 toy configurations give 120 pairs. Testing every pair at 0.05 almost guarantees false positives; test the comparisons you planned (the four leave-one-out rows, plus the interactions you suspect), or use a multiple comparison procedure. The ranx library's `compare` runs paired tests across runs: its `stat_test` can be `"student"` (paired t-test, the default), `"fisher"` (randomization, 1000 permutations by default) or `"Tukey"` (Tukey's HSD across all runs), and its default significance threshold `max_p` is 0.01.

blocks.code:
from ranx import Qrels, Run, compare

qrels = Qrels.from_file("qrels.trec", kind="trec")
runs = [Run.from_file(f"runs/{name}.trec", kind="trec", name=name)
        for name in ["full", "no_Q", "no_H", "no_R", "no_P"]]

report = compare(
    qrels=qrels,
    runs=runs,
    metrics=["ndcg@10", "recall@100"],
    stat_test="fisher",      # paired randomization test
    n_permutations=100_000,  # default is 1000
    max_p=0.01,
)
print(report)
blocks.caption: Leave-one-out runs compared with ranx. Recall@100 at the candidate stage shows whether a first-stage ablation changed what rerankers could see.

blocks.md:
**Cost belongs in the table.** A stage's value is quality per unit of latency or compute. Nogueira et al. measure cost as model inferences per query: $k_0$ for monoBERT and $k_1(k_1-1)$ for duoBERT's all-pairs aggregation. They report that, compared with $k_0 = 1000$, monoBERT achieves more than half the gain with around a fifth of the inferences, and that duoBERT at $k_1 = 20$ gets close to the maximum score with only a 40% latency increase over monoBERT alone.

In the toy, R scores 100 candidates (100 inferences) and P compares all ordered pairs of the top 10 ($10 \times 9 = 90$ inferences). P's Shapley share is 4% of the gain for nearly half of the reranking inferences, a fact the table should show.

Report per-stage deltas with intervals, the paired test and effect size, win/loss counts, interaction cells for stages that depend on each other, and cost, all on one stated harness. A bare column of mean scores invites the wrong conclusion.

blocks.question: Your ablation over 5,000 production queries shows that removing a 30 ms stage lowers nDCG@10 by 0.0008, with p = 0.002. What is the most defensible reading?
options: The stage is clearly valuable because p is far below 0.05
The p-value must be wrong, since such a small delta cannot be significant
Rerun with 20 queries to check whether the effect survives
The effect is probably real but tiny; weigh 0.0008 nDCG (and its interval) against 30 ms per query
blocks.explain: With thousands of queries, tiny differences become significant, as Sakai stresses. Significance says the effect is likely nonzero; the delta, its interval and the cost decide whether it matters. Fewer queries would only lose power.

blocks.question: You ran all 16 configurations of a 4-stage pipeline and tested every pair at alpha = 0.05 with independent paired t-tests. Three pairs come out significant. What is the main concern?
options: Paired t-tests cannot be used for nDCG
With 120 tests, several false positives are expected by chance; plan the comparisons or use a procedure such as Tukey's HSD
Sixteen configurations are too few for a full factorial design
The result is fine as long as the three pairs share a stage
blocks.explain: At 0.05 per test, 120 tests yield about 6 false positives on average even if nothing differs. Restrict to planned comparisons (leave-one-out rows, suspected interactions) or control the familywise error.
